title: Dunbar Residents Association v. City of Vancouver
raw_text: Petition by the Dunbar Residents Association to quash the City of Vancouver's rezoning of 3585 West 41st Avenue from RS-1 to CD-1, which would permit a 12-storey mixed-use building with 148 units. Petitioners argued the rezoning was inconsistent with the Dunbar Community Vision and that City Council failed to give adequate weight to neighbourhood character. The Court dismissed the petition, holding that Council's discretion in land use planning is broad and that the Community Vision is advisory, not binding. The petitioners failed to demonstrate that Council acted in bad faith or outside its statutory authority under the Vancouver Charter. Costs awarded to the City.

title: Heritage Vancouver Society v. City of Vancouver
raw_text: Application for judicial review of the City's decision to remove 2805 West 3rd Avenue (the Chicken Colonel house, circa 1912) from the Vancouver Heritage Register to facilitate redevelopment. Heritage Vancouver Society argued the Director of Planning failed to follow the Heritage Conservation Act procedures and did not adequately consult with the heritage community. The Court found that the Director acted within delegated authority, but ordered the decision set aside on procedural fairness grounds, noting the Society was not given adequate notice or opportunity to make submissions before the removal was finalized. The property was restored to the Heritage Register pending a new review.

title: Marpole Community Coalition v. City of Vancouver
raw_text: Petition challenging the issuance of a development permit for a 28-storey tower at 8460 Granville Street near the Marine Drive SkyTrain station. The Coalition argued that the tower's shadow impacts on adjacent single-family properties were not adequately studied and that the project exceeded the density permitted under the Marpole Community Plan. The Court dismissed the petition, finding that the Development Permit Board had properly considered the urban design panel's recommendations and that the shadow study met the City's guidelines. The Court noted that transit-oriented development near rapid transit stations is an established policy objective under Metro Vancouver's Regional Growth Strategy.

title: Singh v. Board of Variance (City of Vancouver)
raw_text: Appeal from a decision of the BC Supreme Court upholding the Board of Variance's refusal to grant a variance for a secondary suite at 4127 Victoria Drive. The appellant sought to convert a garage into a rental suite with a ceiling height of 6 feet 8 inches, below the 7-foot minimum required by the BC Building Code. The Court of Appeal affirmed the lower court's decision, holding that the Board was correct to refuse the variance on life safety grounds. The Court noted that building code requirements for minimum ceiling height in habitable spaces are not discretionary, and the hardship alleged by the appellant — loss of potential rental income — does not constitute the type of undue hardship contemplated by the Vancouver Charter.

title: Re: 1780 East Broadway Rezoning — Grandview-Woodland Residents v. City of Vancouver
raw_text: Petition to quash the rezoning of 1780 East Broadway from I-1 to CD-1 for a 36-storey mixed-use tower with 350 units. Petitioners, a coalition of Grandview-Woodland residents, argued that the project's density (FSR 7.8) was grossly inconsistent with the Grandview-Woodland Community Plan, that the public hearing was procedurally deficient because virtual participants experienced technical difficulties, and that Council members had a reasonable apprehension of bias due to campaign contributions from the developer. The Court dismissed the petition on all grounds, finding that the Broadway Plan superseded the Community Plan for sites within its boundary, that the City took reasonable steps to accommodate virtual participation, and that the campaign contribution allegations were speculative and unsupported by evidence.

title: Strata Plan BCS 4892 v. Brenhill Developments Ltd.
raw_text: Civil Claim by the strata corporation of a 22-storey residential tower at 6398 Silver Avenue (Metrotown area) against the developer for construction deficiencies. The strata alleged widespread water ingress through the curtain wall system, defective membrane installation on the rooftop amenity deck, and inadequate fire separation between the parkade and residential floors. The plaintiff's expert estimated remediation costs at $14.2 million. The defendant brought an application to strike certain paragraphs of the claim as disclosing no reasonable cause of action. The Court allowed the claim to proceed in its entirety, finding that the allegations, if proven, could ground liability under both the Strata Property Act warranty provisions and the common law duty of care in Winnipeg Condominium.

title: Squamish Nation v. City of Vancouver and TransLink
raw_text: Application by the Squamish Nation for an interlocutory injunction to halt construction of the Broadway Subway extension's ventilation shaft at the corner of Arbutus Street and West 6th Avenue, on the basis that the site is within traditional Squamish territory and that the Crown's duty to consult was not adequately discharged. The Nation argued that archaeological assessments were insufficient and that the project threatened a culturally significant site near the historic village of Sen̓áḵw. The Court granted a temporary injunction for 90 days to allow further archaeological investigation, noting the strength of the Nation's prima facie claim and the irreparable harm that could result from disturbing the site. The Court directed the parties to engage in a structured consultation process overseen by a court-appointed mediator.

title: Re: Bill 47 Transit-Oriented Areas — Kerrisdale Homeowners Coalition v. Province of British Columbia
raw_text: Constitutional challenge to the Transit-Oriented Areas (Bill 47) legislation, brought by a coalition of homeowners near the 41st Avenue SkyTrain stations. The petitioners argued that Bill 47's override of municipal zoning powers violates the constitutional division of powers by effectively expropriating the use and enjoyment of their properties without compensation, and that the resulting density increases (up to 20 storeys within 200m of stations) constitute an unjustifiable infringement of their property rights. The Court dismissed the petition, holding that the Province has plenary authority over municipalities under s. 92(8) of the Constitution Act, 1867, that there is no freestanding constitutional right to property in Canada, and that the legislation serves a valid public purpose of addressing the housing affordability crisis. Leave to appeal was granted.

title: West End Neighbours v. City of Vancouver (View Cone Variance)
raw_text: Judicial review of City Council's decision to grant a view cone variance for a proposed 55-storey tower at 1444 Alberni Street in the West End. The petitioners argued that the project would intrude into protected View Cone 3.2.1 (Queen Elizabeth Park to North Shore Mountains) and that the variance was granted without adequate public consultation. The Court held that Council has discretion to grant view cone variances where, in its judgment, the overall public benefit of the project outweighs the view impact. The Court found that the public hearing process was adequate and that the proposed community amenity contribution of $28 million, including a new childcare facility and social housing units, was a relevant consideration. Petition dismissed with costs.

title: Pacific Environmental Law Centre v. Port of Vancouver
raw_text: Application for judicial review of the Vancouver Fraser Port Authority's environmental assessment decision approving the expansion of the Centerm Container Terminal on Burrard Inlet. The petitioners argued that the assessment failed to adequately consider cumulative effects on the Southern Resident Killer Whale population and underwater noise impacts from increased vessel traffic. The Federal Court found that the Port Authority's assessment was reasonable and that conditions imposed — including vessel speed restrictions and noise monitoring — were adequate mitigation measures. The Court noted, however, that the Port Authority should update its Cumulative Effects Assessment Framework to better account for climate change impacts on marine ecosystems.

title: Strata Plan EPS 7721 (Windfall Tower) — Application for Wind-Up
raw_text: Application under s. 272 of the Strata Property Act for a court-ordered wind-up of Strata Plan EPS 7721, a 45-unit concrete highrise at 1288 West Hastings Street built in 1972. The applicant, holding 82% of the strata votes, sought to dissolve the strata to sell the land to a developer proposing a 42-storey tower. Dissenting owners, comprising 8 units, argued that the wind-up was oppressive and that the proposed compensation of $890,000 per unit was below market value. The Court ordered an independent appraisal and directed that compensation be set at the higher of the appraised value or 110% of BC Assessment value. The wind-up was approved subject to these conditions, the Court finding that the redevelopment served the public interest in housing supply.

title: Chen v. City of Vancouver (Affordable Housing Requirement)
raw_text: Application by a developer challenging the City of Vancouver's requirement that 20% of units in a proposed 18-storey development at 688 West King Edward Avenue be secured as below-market rental for 60 years. The developer argued this condition was ultra vires as an indirect expropriation of property, that it was not authorized by the Vancouver Charter, and that it rendered the project financially unviable. The Court dismissed the application, holding that the City's Inclusionary Housing Policy, enacted pursuant to the Vancouver Charter's broad zoning powers, is a valid exercise of municipal authority. The Court found that the developer voluntarily applied for the rezoning and that density bonusing in exchange for community benefits is a well-established land use tool in Canadian law.

title: Re: Bill 47 TOA Density — Cambie Corridor Alliance v. Province of British Columbia
raw_text: Second constitutional challenge to the Transit-Oriented Areas Act (Bill 47), brought by homeowners along the Cambie Corridor between King Edward and Marine Drive stations. The petitioners alleged that the mandated density increases would cause irreparable harm to neighbourhood character, increase traffic congestion, strain schools and parks, and reduce property values for existing single-family homes. They sought a declaration that Bill 47 is unconstitutional as it applies to established single-family neighbourhoods. The Court followed its earlier ruling in Kerrisdale Homeowners Coalition and dismissed the petition, affirming that the Province's authority over municipalities is constitutionally settled and that policy disagreements about housing density are properly addressed through the political process, not the courts.

title: TransLink v. Owners, 5505-5545 Joyce Street
raw_text: Expropriation proceeding by TransLink for the acquisition of three commercial properties at 5505-5545 Joyce Street, required for the construction of a new bus exchange and transit plaza adjacent to the Joyce-Collingwood SkyTrain station. The property owners challenged the adequacy of compensation, arguing that TransLink's offer of $8.7 million failed to account for the properties' development potential under the Joyce-Collingwood Station Precinct Plan, which would permit up to 18-storey towers. The Expropriation Compensation Board determined fair market value at $12.4 million, applying the highest and best use principle and recognizing the site's transit-oriented development potential. TransLink was ordered to pay the difference plus interest and reasonable legal costs.

title: Kitsilano Heritage Alliance v. City of Vancouver
raw_text: Petition to compel the City of Vancouver to designate the 2300-block of West 4th Avenue as a Heritage Conservation Area under the Vancouver Charter. The petitioners argued that the block, containing six pre-1930 commercial buildings including the former Kitsilano Theatre, met all criteria for heritage designation and that the City's refusal to designate was unreasonable. The Court declined to issue a mandamus order, holding that the decision to designate a Heritage Conservation Area is a discretionary policy decision within Council's sole purview. The Court noted that the Heritage Commission's recommendation in favour of designation was advisory only and did not bind Council. Petition dismissed, but the Court observed that the City's heritage policies could benefit from greater transparency in how designation decisions are communicated.

title: Hastings Sunrise Community Land Trust v. BC Housing
raw_text: Application for judicial review of BC Housing's decision to award the development contract for a 96-unit supportive housing project at 2132 East Hastings Street to a for-profit developer rather than the community land trust. The applicant alleged that the evaluation process was procedurally unfair, that the scoring criteria favoured larger corporate bidders, and that BC Housing failed to give adequate weight to the community land trust's non-profit mandate and local community engagement. The Court found that BC Housing's procurement process was conducted in accordance with its policies and that the scoring was reasonable. However, the Court noted that the evaluation framework did not adequately account for community benefit criteria and recommended that BC Housing review its procurement guidelines for future social housing projects.

title: Kensington-Cedar Cottage Neighbourhood Association v. City of Vancouver
raw_text: Challenge to the development permit for a six-storey rental building at 3456 Knight Street. The Neighbourhood Association argued the project did not comply with the Norquay Village Neighbourhood Centre Plan, specifically regarding required setbacks, and that the parking reduction from 0.8 to 0.4 stalls per unit was unjustified given the distance to the nearest SkyTrain station. The Court found that the Director of Planning acted within delegated authority in granting the parking relaxation, relying on the City's Transportation Demand Management guidelines which support reduced parking near frequent transit. The setback issue was found to be within the permitted range of design flexibility under the plan. Petition dismissed.

title: Musqueam Indian Band v. City of Vancouver and University Endowment Lands
raw_text: Claim by the Musqueam Indian Band asserting Aboriginal title over a 12-hectare parcel in the University Endowment Lands adjacent to Pacific Spirit Regional Park. The Musqueam sought a declaration that the parcel, currently designated as parkland, is unceded Musqueam territory and that any proposed development requires the Band's free, prior and informed consent. The Province intervened, arguing that the claim was premature as the parcel is not currently subject to any development application. The Court declined to grant a declaration at this stage but ordered the parties into a negotiation framework, noting the strength of the Musqueam's historical connection to the area as demonstrated by archaeological evidence of seasonal fishing camps dating to at least 3,000 years ago.

title: Bayshore Towers Strata v. Wesgroup Properties Ltd.
raw_text: Action by the owners of Bayshore Towers (1601 Bayshore Drive) against the developer of an adjacent 38-storey tower at 1650 Bayshore Drive, alleging that construction activities caused structural damage including cracking in the parkade walls, settlement of the foundation, and disruption of the building's waterproof membrane. The plaintiff sought $7.8 million in damages and an injunction to halt further pile-driving. The Court granted a limited injunction requiring the developer to implement vibration monitoring and weekly reporting, but declined to halt construction entirely, finding that an extended stoppage would cause disproportionate harm. The damage claim was set for trial.

title: Re: 550 Pacific Boulevard — False Creek South Residents v. City of Vancouver
raw_text: Petition by False Creek South residents challenging the development permit for a 30-storey residential tower at 550 Pacific Boulevard (Concord Pacific lands). The petitioners argued that the project violated the False Creek North Official Development Plan's height limits and that the environmental assessment failed to consider contaminated soil remediation from the former Expo 86 site. The Court dismissed the petition regarding height, finding the ODP had been properly amended by Council resolution. However, the Court ordered a supplementary environmental site assessment focused on residual contamination from the former industrial use, to be completed before excavation commences. The developer was ordered to bear the cost of the assessment.

title: Shaughnessy Heights Property Owners Association v. City of Vancouver
raw_text: Challenge to the City's approval of a multiplex development at 1489 Osler Street in the Shaughnessy First Shaughnessy District. The petitioners argued that the approval of a four-unit multiplex under the Province's Bill 44 (Small-Scale Multi-Unit Housing) was inconsistent with the First Shaughnessy Official Development Plan and the property's heritage character. The Court held that Bill 44 expressly overrides conflicting municipal zoning, including ODPs, for eligible parcels within urban containment boundaries. The heritage argument was rejected on the basis that the property was not individually listed on the Heritage Register and that the ODP's general neighbourhood character provisions do not constitute heritage designation under the Heritage Conservation Act.

title: Environmental Appeal Board Decision: Burns Bog Conservation Society v. Metro Vancouver
raw_text: Appeal to the Environmental Appeal Board challenging Metro Vancouver's approval of a wastewater treatment outfall extension near Burns Bog in Delta. The Conservation Society argued that increased nutrient loading from the expanded outfall would harm the bog's sensitive peat ecosystem and that the environmental impact assessment understated the risk of eutrophication in adjacent watercourses. The Board upheld the approval with additional conditions, including enhanced effluent quality monitoring, a requirement to achieve tertiary treatment standards within three years, and the establishment of a $2 million environmental mitigation fund. The Board found that the overall benefits of the wastewater infrastructure upgrade to the region's population outweighed the environmental risks, provided the additional conditions were met.

title: Strata Plan LMS 4455 (Pacific Heights) — Application for Court-Ordered Sale
raw_text: Application under s. 280 of the Strata Property Act for a court-ordered sale of all strata lots in Strata Plan LMS 4455, a 60-unit concrete tower at 2055 Pendrell Street in the West End, built in 1968. The applicant, a developer holding 78% of the strata lot votes, sought to acquire the remaining lots to facilitate demolition and construction of a 32-storey tower with 190 units. Twelve dissenting owners opposed the wind-up, citing emotional attachment to their homes, the difficulty of finding comparable housing in the neighbourhood, and concerns about displacement of elderly and fixed-income residents. The Court approved the wind-up subject to enhanced compensation (115% of appraised value), a 12-month relocation period, and a requirement that the developer offer dissenting owners the right of first refusal to purchase units in the new building at a 10% discount.

title: Land Title and Survey Tribunal: Re Application to Cancel Covenant — 3210 Kingsway
raw_text: Application to the Land Title and Survey Tribunal to cancel a restrictive covenant registered against the title of 3210 Kingsway, Collingwood neighbourhood. The covenant, registered in 1956, restricted use of the property to single-family residential purposes. The applicant, who purchased the property in 2022, sought cancellation to develop a six-unit townhouse project permitted under the current RS-1A zoning. The Tribunal granted the application, finding that the covenant was obsolete given the significant changes in the neighbourhood's character since 1956, that the original covenantee's estate could not be located, and that enforcement of the covenant would be contrary to the public interest in housing supply. The Tribunal noted that similar restrictive covenants across Vancouver may face challenges as municipal zoning evolves to permit greater density.

title: City of Vancouver v. Holborn Properties Ltd. (Community Amenity Contribution Appeal)
raw_text: Appeal by the City of Vancouver from a BC Supreme Court decision that the City's Community Amenity Contribution (CAC) negotiation process for a proposed 48-storey tower at 601 West Pender Street constituted an unlawful exaction. The lower court found that the City's demand for a $42 million CAC, equivalent to approximately $180,000 per unit, was disproportionate to the density benefit conferred by the rezoning and amounted to a de facto development charge not authorized by statute. The Court of Appeal reversed, holding that CAC negotiations are voluntary in nature — developers may withdraw their rezoning applications if they find the CAC unacceptable — and that the City's negotiating position was consistent with its published CAC target rates for the downtown peninsula. The Court clarified that CACs are a policy tool, not a tax, and do not require statutory authorization beyond the City's general zoning powers.
